title: Joining the 'Get Happy' TOBA road show with Leonard Reed
summary: In 1927 he joins Happy Donovan and Travis Tucker's TOBA show to Houston, and Clara Donovan hums melodies and stomps tempos for him backstage.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: When did you actually go out, you know, leave home, and...

And really go far away? In 1927 Leonard Reed, who was a dancer, who used to be very, very close to Joe Louis, was in Dallas with his wife. We were naturally at the Ella B. Moore Theater. A show came to town, a traveling show in the TOBA. You know about...you know...well, the TOBA was a circuit similar to the Orpheum Time and various white routes that stars traveled. Well, they had this TOBA-Theatrical Owners' Booking Association. And I was around the theater this night. They needed... usually when guys on the show go from town to town, some guys would quit. A guy may be in St. Louis and he

know that he could get to Dallas in three weeks. Well, he's quitting when he gets to Dallas, that's where he wants to get. So they had lost people on the show and needed people. So Leonard Reed and his wife and myself decided to join Happy Donovan and Travis Tucker's "Get Happy" show and go from Dallas to Houston, because they had contracts and the contract called for 20 people and the man would be at the station and count heads and if you didn't have 20 people he may not pay you. He'd let you sing and dance all the 20 where you're at...where are the people, you know what I mean, your contract called for, for 20 people.
You were leaving Dallas with the...

Road show. All right. Leonard Reed, Ola, his wife, and myself, Happy Donovan, Travis Tucker and a whole slew of TOBA favorites went from Dallas to Houston. Now, I'd been playing shows, you know, amateur for Mrs. Moore, but this was my first professional show. And we rehearsed all day. I...Happy Donovan's wife, Clara, liked me and said that she would help me with the music and I said, "Well, I can't, you know, play by music, you know, there's jazz and stuff. So she says, "what you do, I'll hum," she said, "When a number... when they say, 'and now so-and-so singing the blues.'" She said, "I will start humming backstage and you can

hear me and then you can start from that." And that's how I played the first week with that show, with her help. And when it came to the tempos, she says, "I'll stomp." She'd start...I could hear the tempo and I'd pick the tempo up from her and, you know, and her humming, and start the song. That's how I played my first week as a professional person on TOBA. And after the second week, while we were in Houston, Herschel Thomas--you know who he is?
